source: In the first place, I wish to lay before you a particular, plain statement, touching the living bulk of this leviathan, whose skeleton we are briefly to exhibit. Such a statement may prove useful here.

According to a careful calculation I have made, and which I partly base upon Captain Scoresby’s estimate, of seventy tons for the largest sized Greenland whale of sixty feet in length; according to my careful calculation, I say, a Sperm Whale of the largest magnitude, between eighty-five and ninety feet in length, and something less than forty feet in its fullest circumference, such a whale will weigh at least ninety tons; so that, reckoning thirteen men to a ton, he would considerably outweigh the combined population of a whole village of one thousand one hundred inhabitants.
Think you not then that brains, like yoked cattle, should be put to this leviathan, to make him at all budge to any landsman’s imagination?

Having already in various ways put before you his skull, spout-hole, jaw, teeth, tail, forehead, fins, and divers other parts, I shall now simply point out what is most interesting in the general bulk of his unobstructed bones. But as the colossal skull embraces so very large a proportion of the entire extent of the skeleton; as it is by far the most complicated part; and as nothing is to be repeated concerning it in this chapter, you must not fail to carry it in your mind, or under your arm, as we proceed, otherwise you will not gain a complete notion of the general structure we are about to view.

In length, the Sperm Whale’s skeleton at Tranque measured seventy-two feet; so that when fully invested and extended in life, he must have been ninety feet long; for in the whale, the skeleton loses about one fifth in length compared with the living body. Of this seventy-two feet, his skull and jaw comprised some twenty feet, leaving some fifty feet of plain back-bone. Attached to this back-bone, for something less than a third of its length, was the mighty circular basket of ribs which once enclosed his vitals.

To me this vast ivory-ribbed chest, with the long, unrelieved spine, extending far away from it in a straight line, not a little resembled the hull of a great ship new-laid upon the stocks, when only some twenty of her naked bow-ribs are inserted, and the keel is otherwise, for the time, but a long, disconnected timber.

The ribs were ten on a side. The first, to begin from the neck, was nearly six feet long; the second, third, and fourth were each successively longer, till you came to the climax of the fifth, or one of the middle ribs, which measured eight feet and some inches. From that part, the remaining ribs diminished, till the tenth and last only spanned five feet and some inches. In general thickness, they all bore a seemly correspondence to their length. The middle ribs were the most arched. In some of the Arsacides they are used for beams whereon to lay footpath bridges over small streams.

In considering these ribs, I could not but be struck anew with the circumstance, so variously repeated in this book, that the skeleton of the whale is by no means the mould of his invested form. The largest of the Tranque ribs, one of the middle ones, occupied that part of the fish which, in life, is greatest in depth. Now, the greatest depth of the invested body of this particular whale must have been at least sixteen feet; whereas, the corresponding rib measured but little more than eight feet. So that this rib only conveyed half of the true notion of the living magnitude of that part. Besides, for some way, where I now saw but a naked spine, all that had been once wrapped round with tons of added bulk in flesh, muscle, blood, and bowels. Still more, for the ample fins, I here saw but a few disordered joints; and in place of the weighty and majestic, but boneless flukes, an utter blank!

How vain and foolish, then, thought I, for timid untravelled man to try to comprehend aright this wondrous whale, by merely poring over his dead attenuated skeleton, stretched in this peaceful wood. No. Only in the heart of quickest perils; only when within the eddyings of his angry flukes; only on the profound unbounded sea, can the fully invested whale be truly and livingly found out.
But the spine. For that, the best way we can consider it is, with a crane, to pile its bones high up on end. No speedy enterprise. But now it’s done, it looks much like Pompey’s Pillar.

There are forty and odd vertebræ in all, which in the skeleton are not locked together. They mostly lie like the great knobbed blocks on a Gothic spire, forming solid courses of heavy masonry. The largest, a middle one, is in width something less than three feet, and in depth more than four. The smallest, where the spine tapers away into the tail, is only two inches in width, and looks something like a white billiard-ball. I was told that there were still smaller ones, but they had been lost by some little cannibal urchins, the priest’s children, who had stolen them to play marbles with. Thus we see how that the spine of even the hugest of living things tapers off at last into simple child’s play.

modern_en.title: Chapter 103 — Measurement of The Whale’s Skeleton
paragraphs: First of all, I want to give you a detailed, plain account of how big this leviathan is when alive, since we are about to show his skeleton briefly. That account may be useful here.

According to a careful calculation I have made, partly based upon Captain Scoresby's estimate of seventy tons for the largest sized Greenland whale of sixty feet in length, a Sperm Whale of the largest magnitude, between eighty-five and ninety feet in length and something less than forty feet in its fullest circumference, will weigh at least ninety tons. So that, reckoning thirteen men to a ton, he would considerably outweigh the combined population of a whole village of eleven hundred inhabitants.
Don't you think, then, that brains, like yoked cattle, should be put to this leviathan, to make him budge at all in any landsman's imagination?

I have already shown you, in various ways, his skull, spout-hole, jaw, teeth, tail, forehead, fins and several other parts, so now I will simply point out what is most interesting in the general mass of his bones once they are laid bare. But the colossal skull makes up so very large a share of the whole length of the skeleton, and it is by far the most complicated part, and nothing about it will be repeated in this chapter; so you must be sure to keep it in your mind, or under your arm, as we go on. Otherwise you will not get a complete idea of the overall structure we are about to look at.

In length, the Sperm Whale's skeleton at Tranque measured seventy-two feet. So that when fully fleshed out and extended in life, he must have been ninety feet long, for in the whale the skeleton loses about one-fifth in length compared with the living body. Of this seventy-two feet, his skull and jaw comprised some twenty feet, leaving about fifty feet of plain backbone. Attached to this backbone, for something less than a third of its length, was the mighty circular basket of ribs that once enclosed his vital organs.

To me this vast chest with its ivory ribs, and the long, plain spine running far away from it in a straight line, looked a good deal like the hull of a great ship just laid down on the stocks, when only about twenty of her bare bow-ribs have been set in place and the keel, for the moment, is otherwise just a long, unconnected timber.

There were ten ribs on each side. The first, counting from the neck, was nearly six feet long. The second, third and fourth each got longer in turn, up to the high point of the fifth, one of the middle ribs, which measured eight feet and a few inches. From there the remaining ribs grew shorter, until the tenth and last spanned only five feet and a few inches. Their thickness was generally in proportion to their length. The middle ribs had the greatest curve. On some of the Arsacides, ribs like these are used as beams to lay footbridges across small streams.

Looking at these ribs, I was struck once again by the point this book has made in so many ways: the whale's skeleton is by no means a mold of his body as it is when clothed in flesh. The largest of the Tranque ribs, one of the middle ones, sat in the part of the fish that is deepest in life. Now, the greatest depth of this particular whale's body, fully clothed, must have been at least sixteen feet, while the matching rib measured only a little over eight. So this rib gave only half a true idea of how big that part was in the living animal. What's more, for some distance along where I now saw only a bare spine, all of it had once been wrapped in tons of extra bulk in the form of flesh, muscle, blood and bowels. Furthermore, in place of the broad fins I saw here only a few jumbled joints, and in place of the heavy, majestic, but boneless flukes, nothing at all!

How vain and foolish, then, I thought, for timid, untraveled man to try to comprehend this wondrous whale rightly by merely poring over his dead, shrunken skeleton, stretched in this peaceful wood. No. Only in the heart of the quickest perils, only when within the swirling of his angry flukes, only on the profound unbounded sea, can the fully living whale be truly found out.

But the spine. For that, the best way to consider it is with a crane, to pile its bones high up on end. No speedy enterprise. But now that it's done, it looks much like Pompey's Pillar, the ancient column at Alexandria.

There are forty-odd vertebrae altogether, and in the skeleton they are not locked together. Most of them lie like the great knobbed blocks of a Gothic spire, forming solid layers of heavy masonry. The largest, one in the middle, is a little under three feet wide and more than four feet deep. The smallest, where the spine narrows into the tail, is only two inches wide and looks rather like a white billiard ball. I was told there had been even smaller ones, but some little cannibal urchins, the priest's children, had stolen them to play marbles with, and they were lost. So we see that the spine of even the hugest living thing tapers off in the end into simple child's play.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 103 — Måling af hvalens skelet
paragraphs: Først vil jeg give dig en udførlig, jævn beretning om, hvor stor denne leviatan er i live, eftersom vi nu kort skal vise hans skelet. Den beretning kan være nyttig her.

Efter en omhyggelig beregning, jeg har foretaget, delvis bygget på kaptajn Scoresbys skøn på halvfjerds tons for den største grønlandshval på tres fods længde, vil en kaskelot af den største størrelse, mellem femogfirs og halvfems fod lang og med noget under fyrre fods omkreds på det tykkeste sted, veje mindst halvfems tons. Så når man regner tretten mand på et ton, ville han veje betydeligt mere end hele befolkningen i en landsby på elleve hundrede indbyggere.
Synes du så ikke, at man burde spænde hjerner for denne leviatan som åg-okser, for at få ham til overhovedet at rokke sig i nogen landkrabbes forestilling?

Jeg har allerede vist dig hans kranium, blæsehul, kæbe, tænder, hale, pande, finner og adskillige andre dele på forskellig vis, så nu vil jeg blot pege på det mest interessante i den samlede masse af hans knogler, når de er blottet. Men det kolossale kranium udgør en så stor del af skelettets hele længde, og det er langt den mest indviklede del, og intet om det vil blive gentaget i dette kapitel; så du må sørge for at holde det i erindring eller have det under armen, mens vi går videre. Ellers får du ikke et fuldstændigt billede af den samlede opbygning, vi nu skal se på.

Kaskelotskelettet på Tranque målte to og halvfjerds fod i længde. Så når han var fyldt ud med kød og strakt ud i live, må han have været halvfems fod lang, for hos hvalen mister skelettet omkring en femtedel af længden i forhold til det levende legeme. Af disse to og halvfjerds fod udgjorde kranium og kæbe omkring tyve fod, så der var omkring halvtreds fod ren rygrad tilbage. Fæstet til denne rygrad, over noget under en tredjedel af dens længde, sad den vældige runde kurv af ribben, der engang havde omsluttet hans livsvigtige organer.

For mig lignede dette vældige bryst med sine elfenbensribben og den lange, nøgne rygsøjle, der løb i en lige linje væk fra det, ganske meget skroget på et stort skib, der netop er lagt på stabelen, når kun omkring tyve af de nøgne stævnspanter er sat på plads, og kølen for øjeblikket ellers bare er et langt, usammenhængende stykke tømmer.

Der var ti ribben på hver side. Det første, regnet fra halsen, var næsten seks fod langt. Det andet, tredje og fjerde blev hver især længere, op til højdepunktet ved det femte, et af de midterste ribben, som målte otte fod og nogle tommer. Derfra blev de resterende ribben kortere, indtil det tiende og sidste kun spændte fem fod og nogle tommer. Deres tykkelse stod som regel i forhold til deres længde. De midterste ribben havde den største krumning. På nogle af Arsacides-øerne bruges den slags ribben som bjælker til at lægge gangbroer over små vandløb.

Da jeg så på disse ribben, slog det mig endnu en gang, hvad denne bog på så mange måder har fremhævet: Hvalens skelet er på ingen måde en afstøbning af hans krop, sådan som den er, når den er iklædt kød. Det største af Tranque-ribbenene, et af de midterste, sad i den del af fisken, der er dybest, mens dyret lever. Nu må den største dybde af netop denne hvals krop, fuldt iklædt, have været mindst seksten fod, mens det tilsvarende ribben kun målte lidt over otte. Så dette ribben gav kun et halvt sandt billede af, hvor stor den del var på det levende dyr. Desuden havde alt det, jeg nu kun så som bar rygrad, over en strækning engang været omviklet med tonsvis af ekstra masse i form af kød, muskler, blod og indvolde. Og i stedet for de brede finner så jeg her kun nogle få rodede led, og i stedet for de tunge, majestætiske, men benløse haleflipper — slet ingenting!

Hvor nytteløst og tåbeligt, tænkte jeg da, at den frygtsomme, ubereiste menneskeslægt forsøger at begribe denne vidunderlige hval ret ved blot at stirre på hans døde, sammenskrumpede skelet, udstrakt i denne fredfyldte skov. Nej. Kun i hjertet af de hurtigste farer, kun inde i hvirvlen fra hans vrede haleflipper, kun på det dybe, grænseløse hav kan den fuldt levende hval virkelig udforskes.

Men rygsøjlen. Den bedste måde at betragte den på er med en kran, så man stabler dens knogler højt op på højkant. Intet hurtigt foretagende. Men nu, hvor det er gjort, ligner den meget Pompeius' Søjle, den antikke søjle i Alexandria.

Der er i alt godt fyrre ryghvirvler, og i skelettet er de ikke låst sammen. De fleste af dem ligger som de store knudrede blokke i et gotisk spir og danner solide lag af tungt murværk. Den største, en i midten, er lidt under tre fod bred og over fire fod dyb. Den mindste, der hvor rygsøjlen smalner ind til halen, er kun to tommer bred og ligner snarere en hvid billardkugle. Jeg fik at vide, at der havde været endnu mindre, men nogle små kannibalske knægte, præstens børn, havde stjålet dem for at spille klink med dem, og de var gået tabt. Så vi ser, at rygsøjlen hos selv det største levende væsen til sidst løber ud i simpel børneleg.
